purpose: Teach the water, energy, carbon, hardware, and infrastructure footprint of AI using transparent system boundaries, measured data, uncertainty, location, time, and comparison.
staffSummary: Build M62 around one consequential utility situation and one decision: Decide what environmental evidence an AI investment or procurement decision requires and what reduction options are credible. The learner must leave with a usable AI sustainability boundary and measurement plan, not a collection of definitions.
openingSituation: A sustainability claim cites one global estimate without naming the model, workload, data center, cooling system, grid, water source, location, or time period.
learnerDecision: Decide what environmental evidence an AI investment or procurement decision requires and what reduction options are credible.
analogy: A water audit is useful only when the system boundary and balance are clear. AI footprint claims need the same accounting discipline.
learnerOutcomes: Explain AI Sustainability: The Water & Energy Footprint of AI in plain English and connect it to a real water, wastewater, stormwater, or One Water decision.
Distinguish withdrawal, consumption, energy use, carbon intensity, embodied impact, workload, allocation, boundary, and uncertainty without using one term to hide several different jobs.
Analyze the module situation, identify missing evidence, and name the professional consequence of a weak decision.
Compare how the same question changes across drinking water, wastewater, stormwater, administration, engineering, finance, technology, and public leadership.

Evaluate sources, assumptions, limitations, permissions, and human authority using this boundary: Date every footprint figure, show the calculation boundary, avoid false precision, and separate global research from a specific procurement or facility claim.
Create a usable AI sustainability boundary and measurement plan with evidence, roles, limits, review steps, and the next accountable action.
Defend the recommendation to Foundation, Practitioner, and Leader audiences while keeping disagreement and uncertainty visible.
curriculumOutcomes: Give AI Sustainability: The Water & Energy Footprint of AI one clear learning job inside AI Across the Water Lifecycle.
Connect the module to a consequential decision and the AI sustainability boundary and measurement plan.
Preserve current content, proposals, enhancements, and contributor records by stable identifier.
Separate verified evidence, Hardeep positions, expert interpretation, instructional scenarios, and unresolved questions.
Create an explicit bridge to the preceding and following modules without duplicating their work.
marketingOutcomes: Describe the practical value as helping a learner make and explain this decision: Decide what environmental evidence an AI investment or procurement decision requires and what reduction options are credible.
Name the AI sustainability boundary and measurement plan as the visible result of the module.
Do not promise savings, compliance, certification, safety, performance, implementation success, or career outcomes without separately approved evidence.
requiredWorkProduct: AI sustainability boundary and measurement plan
definitionOfDone: The learner explains the core distinctions, completes the required evidence and decision activities, passes distributed checks, saves a complete AI sustainability boundary and measurement plan, and names the next accountable action.
scopeBoundary: Date every footprint figure, show the calculation boundary, avoid false precision, and separate global research from a specific procurement or facility claim.
researchQuestions: What must an intelligent newcomer understand about AI Sustainability: The Water & Energy Footprint of AI before using it in utility work?
Which sources can support the distinctions among withdrawal, consumption, energy use, carbon intensity, embodied impact, workload, allocation, boundary, and uncertainty?
What evidence would allow a practitioner to make this decision: Decide what environmental evidence an AI investment or procurement decision requires and what reduction options are credible.
Which failure modes, counterexamples, and edge conditions could make the AI sustainability boundary and measurement plan misleading?
How does the question change across drinking water, wastewater, stormwater, reuse, finance, engineering, administration, technology, and public accountability?
Which actions require qualified operator, engineer, water-quality, cybersecurity, privacy, legal, procurement, records, finance, accessibility, or executive review?
